summary: Specifies the gopher URI scheme, previously described in RFC 1738. It was written so that RFC 1738 could be made obsolete while the scheme's description stays on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Gopher was an early way to browse menus on the internet. This memo keeps the rules for gopher-style web addresses written down.

questions: how to write a gopher url
what is the gopher uri scheme
what is the default gopher port
subtitle: How to write a web-style address that points at a Gopher menu, document or search.

tldr.problem: RFC 1738 was being made obsolete, but the description of the gopher URL scheme in it still needed a home on the standards track.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4266 copies the scheme over: a gopher URL names a host, an optional port (default 70), a one-character Gopher type and a selector, with optional search and Gopher+ parts separated by encoded tabs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1738 could be retired while the gopher scheme stayed standardized. The text itself notes that few Gopher servers are in use today.

today: RFC 4266 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1738 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The text notes that few Gopher servers are in use today.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
Many URI schemes were first defined in RFC 1738. When that document was made obsolete, the scheme definitions in it needed somewhere to live. RFC 4266 copies the gopher scheme out of RFC 1738 so that this material can remain on the standards track.

URIs themselves were defined in RFC 2396, which was updated by RFC 3986. Those documents also say how to define a scheme. This memo only restates the gopher scheme and adds a short historical note.
sections.plainLanguage: An old rulebook was being thrown away. This memo copies the one page about Gopher addresses so it is not lost.

sections.title: The Gopher URL Syntax
sections.content:
The gopher scheme designates Internet resources reachable with the Gopher protocol. The base protocol is described in RFC 1436 and supports items and collections of items (directories). A gopher URL looks like gopher://<host>:<port>/<gopher-path>.

If the port is left out it defaults to 70. The path starts with a gophertype, a single character that says what kind of resource this is, followed by the selector, the string a client sends to the server to say which item it wants. The path may also be empty, in which case the slash is optional and the type defaults to 1.

A selector is a sequence of octets that may contain any octet except tab (09 hexadecimal), LF (0A) and CR (0D). An empty selector is how clients refer to the top-level directory of a server. Some selectors begin with a copy of the type character, so it can appear twice in a row. Within the path, no characters are reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: A Gopher address says which computer to call, then what kind of thing you want, then the name of the exact item. If you give no item, you get the front menu.

sections.title: Searches and Gopher+ Strings
sections.content:
To point at a search on a Gopher search engine, the selector is followed by an encoded tab (%09) and the search string. The client decodes the selector, then sends the selector, a tab and the search string to the server.

The Gopher+ protocol is a set of upward-compatible extensions to the base protocol, described outside the RFC series, that lets items carry attributes and alternate data representations. Gopher URLs for Gopher+ items add a second encoded tab and a gopher+_string. In that case the %09<search> part must be present, although the search itself may be empty.

To fetch a Gopher+ item, the client connects, sends the selector, a tab and the search string (possibly empty), then a tab and the Gopher+ commands.
sections.plainLanguage: A tab in the address is like a divider on a form. After the divider you can add a search word, and after a second divider you can ask for fancier extras.

sections.title: What the Gopher+ String Can Say
sections.content:
The Gopher+ string picks which view or part of an item to use. The text defines these forms:

  • + alone refers to the default view of the item. Directory listings tag Gopher+ items with +.
  • ? alone refers to an item with an electronic form (a +ASK block). Clients fetch the +ASK attribute, have the user fill in the form and return the answers with the selector.
  • ! refers to all attributes of an item, and $ to the attributes of all items in a directory. Adding a name, as in !+ABSTRACT, picks one attribute. Several names are separated by coded spaces.
  • +<view_name>%20<language_name> picks an alternate view, for example +application/postscript%20Es_ES for the Spanish-language PostScript view.

For a filled-in form, the string is a coded version of what the client sends to the server: the selector, a tab, +, a tab and 1, then +-1, the answer values one per line, and a closing line with a single dot, each line ended with CR and LF.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra part of the address is like ordering at a restaurant: the plain dish, the dish in another language, or just a list of its ingredients.

sections.title: Security and Historical Notes
sections.content:
The memo points to RFC 3986 for the many security considerations that apply to URI schemes in general. It adds that the Gopher protocol uses passwords in the clear for authentication and offers no privacy, both of which it calls extremely unsafe in current practice.

The text also includes two historical notes: Gopher was widely implemented in the early 1990s but few Gopher servers are in use today, and Gopher+ was uncommon even when Gopher was popular.
sections.plainLanguage: Gopher sends secrets like a postcard anyone can read, so it is not safe by today's standards. Hardly anyone uses it now.
